workspace_files.data/papers/2212.09251_discovering_lm_be:
Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations
Perez et al., 2022 (arXiv:2212.09251)

Abstract: As language models (LMs) scale, they develop many novel behaviors,
good and bad, exacerbating the need to evaluate how they behave. We automatically
generate evaluations with LMs, creating 154 datasets testing behaviors related to
sycophancy, sandbagging, and stated desires. We discover new cases of inverse
scaling where LMs get worse with size, and instances where RLHF makes models
express stronger political views. Overall, LM-written evaluations are high
quality and let us quickly discover many novel LM behaviors.
workspace_files.data/papers/2310.13548_sycophancy.pdf:
Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
Sharma et al., 2023 (arXiv:2310.13548)

Abstract: Human feedback is commonly utilized to finetune AI assistants, but it
may also encourage model responses that match user beliefs over truthful ones, a
behavior known as sycophancy. We investigate the prevalence of sycophancy in
models whose finetuning procedure made use of human feedback. We find that five
state-of-the-art AI assistants consistently exhibit sycophancy across four varied
free-form text-generation tasks. Our results indicate that sycophancy is a
general behavior of these models, likely driven in part by human preference
judgments favoring sycophantic responses.
workspace_files.docs/reviews/review_alpha.md:
# Review 1: evaluation methodology

Reviewer notes (internal, week of 2026-07-13).

Summary: This review covers evaluation methodology across the recent literature. The main
strengths are careful operationalization and reproducible pipelines. The main
weaknesses are small sample sizes and a reliance on single-model results.

Key points:
- Construct validity is under-argued in most cited works.
- Effect sizes are rarely reported with confidence intervals.
- Recommendation: replicate the two headline results before citing them.

workspace_files.refs/paper_a.md:
# Paper A: sycophancy measurement

Notes on sycophancy measurement (working copy for the related-work section).

Main claim: sycophancy measurement can be measured reliably with model-written test items,
provided quality control filters remove ambiguous items.

Method: 2,000 generated items, filtered to 900 by an LLM judge plus human
spot-checks (kappa = 0.81). Evaluated on two open-weight models.

Result: The measured effect is stable across paraphrases (r = 0.88) but
sensitive to option ordering, suggesting position bias needs explicit controls.

workspace_files.refs/scaling_post_1.md:
# Scaling laws blog post 1: compute-optimal training is misunderstood

Saved from the web, 2026-07-10.

This post argues that compute-optimal training is misunderstood. The author walks through the Chinchilla
compute-optimal framing, then claims that data quality shifts the exponent
more than most replications assume.

Key argument: loss curves alone under-determine the story; downstream task
scaling can diverge from loss scaling by a wide margin.

Takeaway: treat published scaling exponents as dataset-specific, not universal.

# Week 3, lecture 1: experiment design

Course notes (student copy).

Today we covered experiment design. The three things to remember:

1. Definitions first — every metric must have an operational definition.
2. Controls — a result without a null comparison is an anecdote.
3. Replication — fixed seeds and pinned versions, or it did not happen.

Reading for next session: chapter 4, sections 1-3.

workspace_files.data/papers/eval_awareness_pilot.pdf:
Eval-Awareness Pilot Study
Internal draft, 2026

Abstract: We test whether frontier models can distinguish evaluation contexts
from deployment contexts. Across 400 paired prompts, a linear probe on residual
activations separates eval-style from deployment-style inputs with AUROC 0.74.
Behavioral detectors based on self-report underperform the probe (AUROC 0.58).
We discuss implications for benchmark validity and sandbagging detection, and
release the paired-prompt dataset for replication.
workspace_files.data/papers/eval_awareness_followup_prob:
Eval-Awareness Follow-up 1: Probe Generalization
Internal draft, 2026

Abstract: We extend the pilot probe to three held-out model families. Transfer
AUROC drops to 0.61, suggesting the pilot direction is partly model-specific.
A shared subspace across families retains AUROC 0.66. We recommend per-family
calibration before any deployment monitoring use.
workspace_files.data/papers/eval_awareness_followup_beha:
Eval-Awareness Follow-up 2: Behavioral Consistency
Internal draft, 2026

Abstract: We measure whether eval-aware models change their behavior when the
probe indicates awareness. Refusal rates shift by 4.2 percentage points in
flagged contexts (95% CI [1.8, 6.6]). The effect is small but robust to prompt
paraphrase controls, and vanishes under a random-direction control.
workspace_files.summary.md:
# Draft summary: activation steering results

We steered the model along the refusal axis and saw refusal rates
increase monotonically with steering strength. The effect was there
on both harmful and harmless prompts, which suggests that the axis
captures something more like caution than harm detection.

Overall we think these results are pretty solid but the writing here
is rough and could use a clarity pass before it goes to the group.

# Q2 progress report

The pilot ran to completion with fixed seeds. The probe reached
AUROC 0.74 on held-out prompts, beating the self-report baseline
(0.58). Next step is the falsification pass: permutation nulls and
a random-direction control.

Risks: dataset licence unverified; one model family untested.
